# Justice: who holds the power, the numbers, and 2026

Checked: November 10, 2026. Verdict key: CONFIRMED (read on the source page or document) / CONFIRMED, SECONDARY (the figure is attributed to another body) / DISAGREE (sources conflict; the page shows the range) / NOT USED.

Access limits: Stateline's public-defender story, the Campaign Zero landing page, Wisconsin Examiner and WBUR returned HTTP 403 or no results to the fetch tool. The BJS sheriffs bulletin and the Mapping Police Violence report are PDFs; their text was extracted with a free tool and read. Ballotpedia's "Judicial selection" page returned empty, so the Brennan Center's "Judicial Selection: Significant Figures" is used for the count of states that elect judges.

## The shape of it

- **Mass Incarceration: The Whole Pie 2026** — Prison Policy Initiative, Wendy Sawyer, Brian Nam-Sonenstein and Peter Wagner, Mar 11, 2026. The U.S. holds "nearly 2 million people" across 1,566 state prisons, 98 federal prisons, 3,116 local jails, 1,277 juvenile facilities, 220 immigration detention facilities and 77 Indian country jails (plus military prisons, civil commitment centers, psychiatric facilities and territorial prisons). System-wide cost "at least $445 billion each year." Pretrial: 465,000 people (426,000 in local jails, 24,000 federal, 1,300 Indian country, 13,000 youth); about 120,000 people in jail on a given day have been convicted, "generally of misdemeanors with sentences under a year." Federal prisons: 153,238 in Bureau of Prisons custody (Jan 27, 2026). ICE average daily population 68,990 (Jan 7, 2026). Youth: 34,000 (Census of Juveniles in Residential Placement, Oct 2023). ICE detention rose 58% (25,200 people) between 2025 and 2026; "expanded immigration detention accounts for virtually all of the growth in mass incarceration since our last report." Corrections spending rose $24.8 billion (27%) from 2017 to 2025 while confined populations shrank; federal immigration policing and detention was $54.3 billion in 2025, up from $20 billion in 2017, 13% of government criminal legal system spending. Local jail populations about 12% smaller, and state prisons about 15% smaller, than in 2019. CONFIRMED. The page's text was truncated before the state prison headcount and the grand total, and the remainder of the page does not give them, so the page does not state them. — [Prison Policy Initiative](https://www.prisonpolicy.org/reports/pie2026.html)

## Who holds the power

- **Sheriffs.** BJS, Connor Brooks, "Sheriffs' Offices Personnel, 2020," NCJ 305200, Nov 2022: as of Dec 31, 2020 sheriffs' offices were 20% (2,900) of the more than 14,700 general-purpose law enforcement agencies and employed 25% (174,000) of the 708,000 full-time sworn officers and 55% (191,000) of the civilian personnel; 76% employed fewer than 50 full-time-equivalent sworn officers; about 10% of full-time sworn officers were assigned to jail-related duties. CONFIRMED. — [BJS bulletin (PDF, as mirrored)](https://30x30initiative.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Sheriffs-Offices-Personnel-2020.pdf). BJS press release, June 16, 2016: sheriffs' offices are "typically directed by an elected official," and "most also operate local jails" (3,012 offices and about 189,000 sworn officers on Jan 1, 2013). CONFIRMED. — [BJS](https://bjs.ojp.gov/press-release/sheriffs-office-personnel-1993-2013)
- **Prosecutors.** UNC Carolina Law Prosecutors and Politics Project, May 13, 2026: local prosecutor elections were held in 45 states in 2020–2024, 3,231 regular elections; 23% were contested, down from 27% in 2018–2019 and 30% in 2014–2017; "voters had less choice than in any cycle" the Project has examined; a decade of races across 2,340 jurisdictions. The page names no authors besides director Carissa Byrne Hessick. CONFIRMED. — [Carolina Law](https://law.unc.edu/?p=17154). Bolts, Daniel Nichanian, Apr 10, 2026: all 15 of Oregon's 2026 district attorney races are uncontested (12 incumbents, three chief deputies); the only cycle since 2000 in which all of Oregon's DA races were uncontested; five of the 12 incumbents first got the office by gubernatorial appointment. CONFIRMED. — [Bolts](https://boltsmag.org/oregon-uncontested-da-elections/)
- **Judges.** Brennan Center, "Judicial Selection: Significant Figures" (published May 8, 2015; updated Apr 14, 2023): 39 states use some form of election at some level of court; of the 38 states that use elections for high-court judges, 16 appoint and then use unopposed retention elections, 14 use contested nonpartisan elections and 8 contested partisan; trial judges are chosen in nonpartisan elections in 21 states and partisan elections in 11. CONFIRMED (dated 2023). — [Brennan Center](https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/judicial-selection-significant-figures)

## Prosecutors and pleas

- **Pew Research Center, June 11, 2019 (fiscal 2018 federal data from the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts):** about 2% of roughly 80,000 federal defendants went to trial; about 90% pleaded guilty; about 8% had cases dismissed; 320 of 79,704 defendants were acquitted at trial (under 1%). State figures are "harder to come by"; trial rates "tend to be very low"; in 2017, jury trials were fewer than 3% of criminal dispositions in 22 jurisdictions with data (Texas 0.86%, New York 2.91%), per the National Center for State Courts. The "trial penalty" is a critics' concept from a 2018 National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers report, not a finding on the page. CONFIRMED (2018 data). — [Pew](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2019/06/11/only-2-of-federal-criminal-defendants-go-to-trial-and-most-who-do-are-found-guilty/)

## Sheriffs and ICE

- **NPR (via HPPR), Feb 17, 2026:** as of Feb 13, ICE reported 1,412 active 287(g) agreements across 40 states and territories; "more than 1,130" were signed in 2025 alone; in 2019 "just 45" were signed. Three models: jail enforcement (everyone booked into a local jail is checked for legal status), warrant service officer, and task force (officers "can stop, question and make arrests for immigration violations," with ICE supervisor approval per DHS). ICE offers "full reimbursements" for the salary and benefits of each trained officer, overtime up to 25%, and quarterly performance awards. Florida's governor has "effectively required" local agencies to sign; Virginia's governor ordered state agency agreements terminated; a Maryland bill to ban them was headed to the governor (outcome not on the page). Critics: UC Irvine law professor Annie Lai ("the potential for civil rights violations is acute"); GAO says the program needs better oversight; DHS calls racial profiling allegations "categorically FALSE"; Heritage's Simon Hankinson calls the concerns "overblown." CONFIRMED. — [NPR via HPPR](https://www.hppr.org/npr-news/2026-02-17/little-used-ice-agreements-with-local-police-have-exploded-under-trump)
- **Texas.** WJLA, July 18, 2025: counties that run or contract out a jail must join the 287(g) program; the law takes effect Jan 1, 2026 with compliance required by Dec 1, 2026; annual compliance reports; the Attorney General "may initiate enforcement actions against sheriffs who fail to comply"; a bill author says it applies to 234 of 254 counties. Opponents worry about racial profiling and costs; supporters say it helps local agencies assist federal enforcement. CONFIRMED as of July 2025 (the article's own date). — [WJLA](https://wjla.com/news/nation-world/a-new-law-requires-texas-sheriffs-to-work-with-ice-these-counties-are-already-signed-up)
- A later search summary gave 2,506 active agreements as of Sept 14, 2026 (a Latin Times item; not read) and a Maryland ban facing lawsuits (not read). NOT USED; the page uses the NPR count and dates it.

## Jails and bail

- Prison Policy Initiative figures above. "Since 1997, all of the net growth in jails came from the pretrial population" (PPI graph, 2026; recorded in municipal_framework.md, Section E).
- **Illinois.** Capitol News Illinois, Peter Hancock, Sept 13, 2024: the Pretrial Fairness Act ended cash bail, upheld 5–2 by the Illinois Supreme Court in July 2023, effective Sept 18, 2023; "the first state in the nation to eliminate the use of cash bail." Loyola University research, preliminary, first year: jail populations fell "but nowhere near as much" as predicted; failure-to-appear rate about 17% before and about 15% after; no documented increase in crime comparing the first six months of 2023 with 2024 (statewide, in Chicago, other urban and rural areas, violent or property crime); detention hearings in urban counties rose from a median four minutes to 16; "We can't say whether it's had an impact on crime." CONFIRMED (the evidence is early and the researchers say so). — [Capitol News Illinois](https://capitolnewsillinois.com/news/a-year-after-end-of-cash-bail-early-research-shows-impact-less-than-many-hoped-or-feared/). Not used: a July 2026 court-watching report on Cook County detention hearings (Illinois Network for Pretrial Justice, 73.8% detention in 167 observed hearings) and an Illinois Policy Institute analysis; seen only in search summaries.

## Courts and judges, 2026

- **Brennan Center State Court Report, Alicia Bannon and Douglas Keith, Nov 4 (updated Nov 5), 2026.** Texas Supreme Court: Democratic challengers defeated all four Republican justices seeking reelection, including Chief Justice Jimmy Blacklock (lost to Maggie Ellis); the court now has a "narrow 5–4" Republican majority. Texas Court of Criminal Appeals: Audra Riley beat Kevin Yeary; Holly Taylor and Okey Anyiam won two open seats; 6–3 Republican majority. Ohio Supreme Court: Jennifer Brunner kept her seat and Marilyn Zayas beat Justice Daniel Hawkins; Democrats gained a seat; Republicans keep a 5–2 majority. North Carolina: Anita Earls won reelection over Sarah Stevens; 5–2 Republican majority; the race drew over $8 million and is on track to be the year's most expensive state supreme court election. Montana: Amy Eddy beat Dan Wilson; a citizens' initiative to put nonpartisan judicial elections into the constitution passed with 68%. The authors say the results "are not likely to immediately change any state high court majorities" and set up 2028. No margins given for most races; no Michigan or Washington results in the article. CONFIRMED. — [State Court Report](https://statecourtreport.org/our-work/analysis-opinion/state-supreme-court-election-results-tee-fights-court-majorities-2028)
- **Wisconsin 2025:** about $57 million in outside spending (Brennan Center, as cited by the Roosevelt Institute report, Oct 2025). CONFIRMED, SECONDARY. A search summary also reports a Wisconsin race in April 2026 won by Chris Taylor for a 5–2 liberal majority with sharply lower spending; the pages were not read (Wisconsin Examiner returned 403). NOT USED.
- **Kansas:** voters rejected the amendment to elect justices on Aug 4, 2026 (research already on the page; municipal_framework.md, Section D).

## Public defense

- **Vera Institute, Nazish Dholakia, Feb 17, 2026:** indigent defense "chronically under-resourced for decades," funded at "drastically lower levels" than law enforcement and prosecutors (no dollar figures on the page); "one-third to half" of people who qualify are represented by assigned or contract counsel (estimate; no year or named source); in 1963 the Supreme Court held that a poor person's trial "cannot be assured a fair trial unless counsel is provided." Every state now contributes some indigent defense funding, a milestone in March 2024 (unnamed source). CONFIRMED as the page's own statements. — [Vera](https://vera.org/news/public-defenders-are-underfunded)
- **Spotlight PA, Danielle Ohl, Apr 1, 2026:** Pennsylvania was for decades "one of only two states" that did not fund public defense; counties are still the primary funder; the state approved $7.5 million in 2023 and again in 2024 and 2025, split across 67 counties; a committee analysis found the state "about 400 attorneys short" for adult criminal cases; nearly 40% of attorneys hired in the past five years have left; in up to 20% of cases records showed no or "unknown" representation (the article says the data may be incomplete); the ACLU of Pennsylvania sued in 2024 and the case is ongoing. CONFIRMED. — [Spotlight PA](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2026/04/pennsylvania-indigent-defense-public-defender-state-funding-justice-system/)
- Not used: Texas "lost 1,345 indigent-defense attorneys" and New Mexico's "21.6% vacancy rate" (seen only in search summaries; the Stateline page returned 403); a national shortage figure (a researcher called it "a complete black box").

## Police, force and accountability

- **Mapping Police Violence / Campaign Zero, "U.S. Police Violence in 2025," year-end report (last updated Feb 2026):** police killed at least 1,314 people in 2025, a 5% decrease from 1,383 in 2024, the first decrease in six years; an average of 3.6 per day; since 2019 officers have been charged with a crime after a killing "with increasing frequency"; the organisation warns federal agencies are expanding use of force and some states are rolling back reforms such as restrictions on vehicle pursuits. The data come from news articles verified by researchers plus official sources. CONFIRMED (read in full). **DISAGREE:** other outlets cite 1,201 or 1,202 for 2025 (seen in search summaries); the page uses Mapping Police Violence's own count. — [Mapping Police Violence](https://www.mappingpoliceviolence.org/files/mpv-year-end-report-2025.pdf)
- **Zorn v. Linton, No. 25-297, decided Mar 23, 2026** (Dorsey client alert): per curiam; a Vermont sergeant used a rear wristlock on a protester at a State House sit-in; the Court reversed the Second Circuit and held he was entitled to qualified immunity because no earlier case clearly established that his conduct violated the Fourth Amendment; courts generally "need to identify a case where an officer acting under similar circumstances … was held to have violated" the Constitution. Justice Sotomayor, joined by Justices Kagan and Jackson, dissented. CONFIRMED. — [Dorsey](https://www.dorsey.com/newsresources/publications/client-alerts/2026/3/march-23-supreme-court-update)

## Crime trends

- **Council on Criminal Justice, July 23, 2026 (mid-year 2026):** 36 cities, 13 offenses (homicide uses 30 cities). Homicides down 18% in the first half of 2026 from the first half of 2025, 51% below the 2022 peak, and 31% below the first half of 2019; carjacking down 47% (the largest drop); drug offenses up 12% (the largest rise); domestic violence up 8%. The 2025 national homicide rate was estimated at about 4.0 per 100,000, which would be the lowest since at least 1900 if FBI data confirm it. "There is no single or easy explanation"; "This report is not evidence of the success or failure of any policy or practice"; the cities are not necessarily representative. CONFIRMED. — [Council on Criminal Justice](https://counciloncj.org/homicide-likely-reaching-a-new-historic-low-as-most-crime-rates-continue-to-decline-at-mid-year/)

## Who is affected, and who can vote

- **The Sentencing Project, Oct 29, 2026:** about four million Americans were denied the right to vote because of a felony conviction in the 2024 federal election; about one in 22 voting-age Black Americans is blocked from the ballot, more than three times the rate of non-Black Americans; Maine, Vermont, Puerto Rico and Washington, D.C. allow citizens to vote while incarcerated; Missouri restored voting rights to more than 41,000 people on felony probation and parole; a federal court ruling sharply narrowed Virginia's policy. CONFIRMED. — [The Sentencing Project](https://www.sentencingproject.org/press-releases/midterm-elections-highlight-efforts-to-end-felony-disenfranchisement-nationwide/)
- **Virginia amendment, Nov 3, 2026:** "More than 56% of voters said 'yes'"; it will "automatically restore voting rights to people with felony convictions when they leave prison" (previously people had to petition the governor); "The change takes effect Jan. 1" (year not stated on the page). CONFIRMED (early reporting, 12 On Your Side, Nov 6; not the certified count). — [12 On Your Side](https://www.12onyourside.com/2026/11/06/virginia-voters-approve-amendment-restoring-voting-rights-after-felony-convictions/)
- **The Sentencing Project, "The Color of Justice," Oct 13, 2021** (data from BJS "Prisoners in 2019"): Black Americans are imprisoned at nearly five times the rate of white Americans; Latino Americans at 1.3 times; one in 81 Black adults is serving time in state prison; Black/white disparity larger than 9 to 1 in California, Connecticut, Iowa, Maine, Minnesota, New Jersey and Wisconsin; nine states cut prison populations by 30% or more. CONFIRMED but old; the page says so. **DISAGREE:** a Prison Policy Initiative page gives about six times (seen in a search summary). — [The Sentencing Project](https://www.sentencingproject.org/reports/the-color-of-justice-racial-and-ethnic-disparity-in-state-prisons-the-sentencing-project/)
- Jail voting (Massachusetts 1% and 5%; Harris County) is on the page already (municipal_framework.md, Section E).

## From the editor's analytical framework (Downloads: "Justice Webpage Analytical Framework.md"), checked Nov 10, 2026

The framework's inline numbers are not sourced to specific pages and some are garbled in the file, so each claim was checked against its cited source or the original. Used only where confirmed.

- **Jail voting, Cook County.** Prison Policy Initiative, Naila Awan, Oct 25, 2022: in the June 2022 primary "roughly 25% of people detained at the jail" (1,384 of 5,560) voted, higher than registered-voter turnout in Chicago (20%); about half used same-day registration; Cook County 2020 general: more than 2,000 of about 5,400 (roughly 37%); Cook County 2018 primary: 394 (under 7%) by absentee ballot; Will County June 2022 primary: 48 (about 8%); Harris County: 96 voted in Nov 2021 and "13 of the estimated 26 people eligible" in the Mar 1, 2022 primary; jail polling places in Cook, Will, Harris, D.C. (Central Detention Facility), Denver (two facilities) and Los Angeles (Century Regional Detention Facility). CONFIRMED. — [PPI](https://www.prisonpolicy.org/blog/2022/10/25/jail_voting/). Center for Public Integrity, Aaron Mendelson, Sept 15, 2022: about 445,000 unconvicted people in jails and about 100,000 serving misdemeanor sentences (2022 figures); the average jail stay is 28 days; jail is not a recognized absentee excuse in several states; Cook County officials estimate 80% of people in their jail are eligible; Cook's jail has been a polling place since 2020 under a 2019 law. CONFIRMED (already a source on the page). **Not used:** the framework's "typical jail turnout is 1% to 5%." No source gives that as a national finding; 1% and 5% are the Massachusetts 2024 figures already on the page, and the Cook and Will County figures above are higher.
- **O'Brien v. Skinner, 414 U.S. 524 (decided Jan 16, 1974)** (Cornell LII). New York's election laws let some voters register and vote absentee but not inmates confined in their county of residence (72 people held in the Monroe County jail, awaiting trial or serving misdemeanor sentences); the Court held this denied equal protection, "wholly arbitrary" as applied to them, because they were "denied any alternative means of casting their vote." It said the case fell within the "fact structure that the McDonald holding foreshadowed"; the opinions quote *McDonald v. Board of Election Commissioners* (1969) as treating the claim as "a claimed right to receive absentee ballots" with "nothing in the record to show that appellants (were) in fact absolutely prohibited from voting by the State." CONFIRMED. The framework's wording ("the Court required states only to refrain from explicitly blocking every avenue") is a law-review characterization; the page uses the Court's own words and says McDonald was read only as quoted in O'Brien. O'Brien concerned New York's election laws and the Monroe County, New York jail. — [Cornell LII](https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/414/524)
- **Sheriff campaign money.** Common Cause and Communities for Sheriff Accountability, "The Paid Jailer: How Sheriff Campaign Dollars Shape Mass Incarceration" (copyright Dec 2021, edited Jan 18, 2022; authors Jonathan Henry, Keshia Morris Desir, Max Rose, Beth Rotman, Paul S. Ryan). Data sought from 105 sheriffs; research in 11 states and "less than 3 percent of sheriffs offices"; "approximately 13,000 apparent conflicts of interest, primarily between 2010 and 2021"; "upward of $6 million, approximately 40% of all examined contributions" (about $15.7 million total); conflicts defined by the authors as contributions from incarceration-specific businesses and from others that may benefit from business with a sheriff's office (construction, food services, weapons manufacturers); sheriffs selected by "a combination of public interest, and random selection"; the authors "did not attempt to determine the legality of specific contributions and contracts"; of 105 tracked FOIA requests sheriffs' offices acknowledged 55. Examples: CPS Healthcare spent more than $20,365 on Massachusetts sheriffs' campaigns ($12,040 to Bristol County's sheriff) and Massachusetts sheriffs paid it $9.82 million in contracts from 2012 to 2021; Maryland sheriffs up to $1,396,569 across 24 campaigns; Massachusetts up to $2,686,129 across 13 sheriffs' campaigns; the Orange County (CA) sheriff $715,000. CONFIRMED (read in full), advocacy-group report. Not used: the report's statement that roughly 90% of sheriffs are white men and its jail-population figures (2021). — [Common Cause](https://www.commoncause.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/01/CC_PaidJailer_WEB_FINAL.pdf)
- **Election-year traffic fines.** Min Su (Louisiana State University) and Christian Buerger (IUPUI), "Playing politics with traffic fines: Sheriff elections and political cycles in traffic fines revenue," *American Journal of Political Science* (blog post May 10, 2024; Early View): "in sheriff election years, traffic fines revenue decreased by 30 percent"; short-lived, "observed only in the election year"; panel of 57 California counties, 2003 to 2020, four election cycles; larger "when an incumbent sheriff sought reelection or when the election was highly contested"; the motive is stated as an expectation ("we anticipate"). CONFIRMED. The framework's "as much as 30%" is the average reported effect, not a maximum. One state. — [AJPS](https://ajps.org/2024/05/10/playing-politics-with-traffic-fines-sheriff-elections-and-political-cycles-in-traffic-fines-revenue/)
- **"Constitutional sheriffs."** Farhang Heydari (Vanderbilt Law School), "The Sheriff's Constitution," Georgetown Law Journal, 2025 (66 pages, text extracted): constitutional sheriffs are "a group of sheriffs who view themselves as the highest authority in their county, answerable only to their electorate," declaring opposition "to gun control measures, pandemic restrictions, environmental protections, and more"; "other sheriffs have declared opposition to immigration and abortion restrictions"; proposes reviving judicially enforceable limits on nonenforcement discretion, modeled on state courts' older supervision of sheriffs' neglect of duty. CONFIRMED. **Not used:** the Barn Raiser opinion piece, the Reddit thread (the framework's source for "sheriffs enjoy a significantly longer average tenure"; no usable source for that claim) and the Wikipedia retention-election page. — [Georgetown Law Journal](https://www.law.georgetown.edu/georgetown-law-journal/wp-content/uploads/sites/26/2025/07/Heydari_The-Sheriffs-Constitution.pdf)
- **Los Angeles County Measure A (Nov 8, 2022).** County press release, Aug 2, 2022: the Board approved an ordinance for a special election on a charter amendment letting it remove a sheriff "for unlawful actions or a violation of statutory duties by a four-fifths vote of the Board"; grounds listed: violating a law related to the performance of a sheriff's duties, flagrant or repeated neglect of duties, misappropriating public funds or property, willfully falsifying a relevant official statement or document, and obstructing an investigation; written notice and an opportunity to be heard, then a public four-fifths vote; the Sheriff Civilian Oversight Commission urged the Board in May 2022 to place a charter amendment on the ballot; motion by Chair Holly J. Mitchell, co-authored by Supervisor Hilda L. Solis. CONFIRMED (pre-election source). LAist (Nov 8–9, 2022): Measure A "has a commanding lead in the votes tallied to date" (no percentages). **Result:** a search summary of Ballotpedia gives 1,633,918 yes (71.84%) to 640,361 no (28.16%); Ballotpedia's page returned empty to the fetch tool, so the page says only that voters approved it. — [Los Angeles County](https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/CALACOUNTY/bulletins/32667b1); [LAist](https://laist.com/news/politics/2022-election-california-general-live-results-los-angeles-county-measure-a)
- **State supreme court money.** Brennan Center, Douglas Keith (research and data analysis by Eric Velasco), "The Politics of Judicial Elections 2023–24," published Feb 26, 2026: at least $157.3 million on state supreme court races, "the most expensive cycle ever," 35% higher than 2019–20 and almost twice 2015–16 (inflation-adjusted); interest groups $85 million (54%) outspent candidates, $70 million (45%), for the first time; parties $2 million independently plus $15 million to candidates in five states ($9 million from the Democratic Party of Wisconsin to Janet Protasiewicz); groups on the left were 64% of interest-group money, with liberal-supporting groups spending $55 million against $30 million for conservative-backed groups; dark money groups on both sides named (A Better Wisconsin Together; WMC; Protect Our Freedoms); Fair Courts America disclosed $9 million of its $12 million from Richard Uihlein; Wisconsin $51 million (2023), Pennsylvania $27 million, North Carolina $10.5 million (state record), Montana $6.8 million and $5.9 million; 30% of 119,000 TV ad spots mentioned abortion rights, against 3% in 2020. CONFIRMED. The framework's "$157 million" and "$85 million against $70 million" are correct (its text garbles the second). — [Brennan Center](https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/politics-judicial-elections-2023-24)
- **Not read or not used from the framework's list:** ACLU of Oregon, "Roadblocks to Reform" (2017), and "How Prosecutor Elections Fail Us" (2009): older than the Carolina Law national study (May 13, 2026) and Bolts (Apr 10, 2026) used on the page, and the claim that most prosecutor races are uncontested is already supported there (77% not contested, 2020 to 2024); the Arkansas Law Review, Harvard CR-CL, St. Mary's and DePaul law articles, the Georgetown ethics paper and the ResearchGate "Shifting Patterns" item: not read; the page does not rely on them. The framework's "600,000 to 746,000 in local jails, 75% to 78% pretrial" is superseded by the 2026 Prison Policy Initiative figures (about 546,000, 78%) on the page.

## Not used

- WBUR's Nov 3, 2026 Massachusetts district attorney results: the fetched page had no results text. A search turned up East Baton Rouge (Hillar Moore re-elected), Cumberland County, Maine (Democrats kept the DA's office) and primary results for Alameda and Wake counties; none read in full, and no national tally of 2026 DA or sheriff results was found. The page says so.
- California Proposition 4 (public financing) and the Michigan and Washington supreme court results: not confirmed.
- The Brennan Center "Nine Solutions" items on justice-related reforms are in money.md (campaign finance only).
